definitions.meaning: The length of a curve along a circle: the angle-over-360 fraction of the full circumference 2 pi r.
A slice of a circle bounded by two radii and an arc; its area is the angle-over-360 fraction of pi r squared.
One third of base area times vertical height: three identical pyramids fill the prism on the same base with the same height.
A perfectly round solid where every surface point is the radius r from the centre; its volume is 4/3 pi r cubed.
The multiplier on lengths when a shape grows; areas multiply by its square and volumes by its cube.

mechanismSteps: Arc length and sector area: a 60 degree sector is 60/360 = 1/6 of the circle, so the arc is 1/6 of 2 pi r and the sector area is 1/6 of pi r squared.
Pyramid volume, revealed: pouring the pyramid into the matching prism takes three full pyramids, so the volume is 1/3 x base area x height.
Sphere volume: stacking thin disk slices of the sphere gives 4/3 pi r cubed; for r = 3 cm that is 36 pi, about 113 cubic centimetres.
A common mistake: doubling r doubles area: growing r from 3 cm to 6 cm fits four small disks inside the big one, so the area goes from 9 pi to 36 pi.
objectives: Find arc lengths and sector areas as fractions of a full circle
Calculate the volume of a pyramid from its base area and vertical height
Use the sphere volume formula and explain why area scales with r squared

title: E-Math mensuration: sectors, pyramids and spheres

trap.explanation: Doubling a length doubles lengths, so area feels like it doubles too. Area scales with the square of the radius: double the radius and the area quadruples. In class, draw circles of radius 3 cm and 6 cm on squared paper: the small disk covers 9 pi worth of squares and the big one 36 pi, and four small disks tile the big one exactly.
trap.misconception: Doubling the radius doubles the area of a circle.

workedExample: Find the arc length and sector area of a 60 degree sector of radius 6 cm. The sector fraction is 60/360 = 1/6. Arc length = 1/6 x 2 pi x 6 = 2 pi, about 6.28 cm. Sector area = 1/6 x pi x 6 squared = 6 pi, about 18.8 square centimetres. Check the trap: the sector area is NOT half of anything to do with doubling - it is the same 1/6 fraction applied to the full circle area.
